summaries.example: Imagine saying, “If we give a plant more water, it will grow taller, other things being equal.” This may work if the plant gets enough sunlight and its roots are healthy. If a pest eats the roots, the result may be different. The phrase helps us remember that a rule can have conditions that are not stated every time.
summaries.summary: Ceteris paribus means “other things being equal.” Scientists often use this idea when a pattern is helpful but not universal. For example, more demand may lead to a higher price when the supply and other important conditions stay suitable. Biology, psychology, and economics contain many such patterns. Philosophers ask whether these patterns should count as laws, what the phrase really means, and whether the patterns can be tested. Some think the missing conditions are disturbing factors that must be absent. Others focus on whether the pattern stays steady in different imagined situations, whether it describes a normal tendency, or whether it describes a power or ability of a system. The central challenge is to avoid making the rule false by ignoring exceptions, while also avoiding a rule so loose that it says almost nothing.
key_ideas: Many rules in biology, psychology, and economics have exceptions, unlike the strict rules traditionally associated with physics.
Scientists use ceteris paribus clauses to say that a pattern works when important conditions are suitable.
Philosophers disagree about what those extra conditions are and whether such rules can be tested.
Some theories explain these rules using stability, normal conditions, tendencies, or changes made by interventions.
summaries.why_it_matters: Ceteris paribus rules are used to make predictions, explain events, and think about what would happen if circumstances changed. Understanding them helps us see why rules from biology, psychology, and economics may work differently from idealized rules in physics. It also reminds us to ask which conditions matter when we apply a scientific idea.

important_terms.definition: A Latin phrase meaning “with other things staying the same” or “when no important interfering factor changes the result.”
A statement that describes a regular pattern in nature or science.
Something that gets in the way of a pattern or changes its result.
A pattern that is not true in every single case but can still help scientists explain or predict what happens.

questions_to_think_about: When does an exception show that a rule is wrong, and when does it show that another factor was present?
Can a rule be useful even if it does not work in every case?
What conditions would you need to keep the same when testing a science rule?

summaries.example: Consider the economic generalization that, under perfect competition, an increase in demand raises a good’s price if supply stays constant. Read strictly, the statement can fail because of regulation, unusual market conditions, or another influence. Read as a ceteris paribus claim, it describes a relationship within a restricted range of circumstances. The philosophical question is whether that restriction identifies a meaningful law, merely protects the statement from any counterexample, or captures a stable relationship useful for intervention and explanation.
summaries.summary: The entry examines how ceteris paribus laws—generalizations qualified by a condition that other relevant things remain equal or suitably arranged—fit into philosophy of science and metaphysics. Traditional laws were often understood as universal and counterfactually supporting, with physics as the model. Yet biology, psychology, and economics use generalizations that are explanatory and predictive while admitting actual and possible exceptions. The debate therefore asks whether these generalizations are laws, what their qualifications mean, and whether they possess non-trivial empirical content. Comparative clauses hold relevant background variables constant; exclusive clauses exclude disturbing factors. Definite clauses specify those factors, whereas indefinite clauses leave them open. Completer theories try to supply omitted conditions, but face worries about vacuity and accidental connections. Stability and invariance theories instead emphasize survival under relevant counterfactual suppositions or interventions. Dispositional theories appeal to tendencies or capacities, while normality theories interpret the qualification through typical conditions or probabilities. Because reasoning from such laws is defeasible, the entry also connects them with non-monotonic logic, ethics, epistemology, and theories of explanation and causation.
key_ideas: Traditional accounts often treat laws as true, universal statements that support counterfactuals; many special-science generalizations do not fit that model.
The main dilemma is that a strict version of a ceteris paribus law may be false, while an unrestricted “unless something interferes” version may be trivial or empirically empty.
Comparative and exclusive readings differ: one holds background variables fixed, while the other excludes disturbing factors. A law can have both features.
Completer theories add missing conditions, but critics argue that they can permit arbitrary or accidental relationships and may fail to provide informative content.
Stability and invariance theories distinguish laws from accidents by asking whether a relationship survives relevant counterfactual changes or interventions.
Normality, dispositional, and non-monotonic approaches offer different accounts of why exception-prone generalizations remain useful in science.
summaries.why_it_matters: The issue matters because scientific explanation and prediction often rely on patterns that are neither strict universal laws nor mere coincidences. A satisfactory account must explain how such patterns can guide inquiry without becoming false through ordinary exceptions or empty through unlimited qualifications. The debate also bears on whether biology, psychology, economics, and other special sciences have their own lawlike generalizations and on how causal reasoning should handle interventions, background conditions, and defeaters.

important_terms.definition: Literally “other things being equal”; in scientific claims, a qualification limiting a generalization to suitable or controlled circumstances.
A general statement that is not true in every actual or possible case, but may still support explanation, prediction, or counterfactual reasoning.
A reading on which unmentioned factors must remain unchanged when two situations are compared.
A reading on which factors capable of disrupting the stated relationship must be absent.
A proposed additional condition that turns an exception-prone generalization into a strict implication.
A property of a generalization whereby it remains true across a relevant range of counterfactual cases or interventions.
An operation that changes a variable while separating that variable from its usual causal influences, allowing its effects to be examined.
A form of reasoning in which a conclusion may be withdrawn when new information reveals an exception or defeater.

questions_to_think_about: Does a clause allowing exceptions preserve a law’s empirical content, or can it make the claim immune to disconfirmation?
Should special-science laws be called laws, or should explanation and causation be understood without universal laws?
How should a theory distinguish a genuine disturbing factor from an ad hoc excuse?
Is a relationship more lawlike because it remains stable under interventions, because it describes normal conditions, or because it expresses a disposition?
Can one general account apply equally well in physics, biology, psychology, and economics?

summaries.example: Suppose a school notices that students who sleep more usually do better on a quiz. This pattern may not hold if students are ill, the quiz is unusually difficult, or the students studied different material. One way to state the claim is, “More sleep improves quiz performance, other relevant things being equal.” Scientists must decide whether this means keeping background conditions similar, excluding particular problems, or describing what normally happens. Each choice affects how the claim can be tested.
summaries.summary: Ceteris paribus is a way of qualifying a scientific rule: the rule is supposed to work when other relevant things are equal, unchanged, or in suitable condition. The idea becomes important because many generalizations in biology, psychology, and economics are useful for explaining and predicting events even though they are not universal. Philosophers disagree about whether such generalizations are genuine laws. One option is to say that only universal laws are laws. Another is to say that explanation does not require laws of that kind. A third is to treat non-universal generalizations as ceteris paribus laws. This third option creates a difficulty. If the rule is treated as strict, an exception makes it false. If the rule simply says it works whenever nothing interferes, it may seem impossible to test and therefore almost empty. Different theories respond in different ways. Completer theories add conditions; stability and invariance theories examine counterfactual changes; dispositional theories appeal to capacities; and normality theories interpret the rule as describing what usually happens. These approaches are connected to causal explanation, counterfactuals, interventions, and reasoning that can be revised when new facts appear.
key_ideas: Physics has often been treated as the model of lawlike science, but successful special sciences use generalizations that have exceptions.
Philosophers face a choice: reject these generalizations as laws, reject the need for universal laws, or accept non-universal laws.
A ceteris paribus clause can mean holding other factors constant or removing factors that would interfere.
If every exception can be explained by adding a new condition, a rule may become too easy to protect and too hard to test.
Some accounts focus on stable counterfactual patterns, while others focus on normality, dispositions, or probabilistic tendencies.
Reasoning with these rules is defeasible: new information can cancel a conclusion.
summaries.why_it_matters: The topic helps explain how scientists use simplified or qualified rules without treating every exception as a complete failure. It also shows why different sciences may need different ideas of lawfulness. Thinking carefully about “other things being equal” can improve experiments, predictions, and arguments by making hidden assumptions visible.

important_terms.definition: A phrase meaning that a claim applies while other relevant things remain the same or suitable.
A broad statement that describes a pattern but allows that some cases may not fit it.
A condition or event that prevents the expected result from occurring.
A rule that holds only when specified conditions are met and listed factors are excluded.
A rule that holds when other variables are kept at the same values in a comparison.
A feature of a pattern that lets it remain true across some imagined changes in circumstances.
A pattern about what usually happens under ordinary or normal conditions.

questions_to_think_about: Would a rule that works most of the time count as a scientific law? Why or why not?
How could researchers test a claim about sleep and quiz performance?
What is the difference between a helpful condition and an excuse added after a prediction fails?
Should “normally” mean statistically common, expected by a reasoner, or something else?
Why might a generalization be useful even when it has exceptions?
